blocks.purpose: Open with a short famous quote (e.g., from a speech) where clickable annotations show how word order and clause choice make it persuasive.

buzzwords.annotation: The subject and verb come first, so the promise lands before the conditions. Word order creates confidence: the reader hears the claim before the obstacles.

blocks.purpose: Define rhetorical grammar: grammar choices (word order, clause type, sentence shape) selected for effect on the reader, with prerequisites on subjects, verbs, and clauses.

data.anchor: Rhetorical grammar means choosing your grammatical structures — word order, clause type, and sentence shape — on purpose, for the effect they create in the reader.
prerequisites: You can find the subject and the verb in any sentence.
You can tell a complete sentence from a fragment by checking for a subject, a verb, and a finished thought.
You know that a run-on is two complete sentences joined without correct punctuation or a connecting word.
You can identify a subordinate clause — one that starts with a word like 'because,' 'although,' or 'if' — and tell it apart from a main clause.

blocks.purpose: Side-by-side comparison of the same idea written flat versus written rhetorically (short fragment punch, periodic build-up, fronted phrase) so the effect is visible.

data.footnote: Rhetorical grammar is a set of choices; a grammatical error is a choice you never meant to make.

items.example: 'The research is clear. Plain and simple.' — short, deliberate, punchy.
items.label: Deliberate fragment
items.text: A short fragment used on purpose for punch, placed after a complete sentence that sets it up.

items.example: 'If we do not act now, the forest will be gone.'
items.label: Periodic build-up
items.text: A sentence that delays the main point to the end so the reader leans forward waiting for it.

items.label: Fronted phrase
items.text: A key phrase moved to the start of the sentence so the reader meets it first.

items.label: Parallel structure
items.text: Matching grammatical forms repeated to build rhythm and credibility.

items.example: 'I missed the bus I was late for class.'
items.label: Accidental fragment or run-on
items.text: A fragment that drops a needed subject or verb by mistake, or a run-on that jams two sentences together without punctuation.

items.example: 'The the result was very unique in every way.'
items.label: Rule-breaking
items.text: Breaking grammar rules without a purpose, which reads as carelessness rather than style.

items.example: 'When considering the matter of the start time, the analysis that was conducted by the committee...' — padding, not power.
items.label: Longer is stronger
items.text: Adding clauses or words just to sound impressive; empty padding weakens persuasion.

items.example: Mixing 'she likes running, swimming, and to bike' breaks the pattern.
items.label: Broken parallelism
items.text: Structures that almost match but don't — the rhythm stumbles and the point wobbles.

blocks.purpose: Walk through four moves in order — say it plain, then front the key phrase, then add the short punch, then end with the strongest point — building one example sentence at each step.

steps.description: 'The team played hard, but they lost the game anyway.' A normal order: subject, verb, detail. Clear, but nothing stands out.
steps.label: Say it plain

steps.description: Spotlight a key phrase by moving it to the front: 'Despite playing hard, the team lost the game anyway.' The reader meets the setback first.
steps.label: Front the key phrase

steps.description: Add a deliberate fragment after a complete sentence for punch: 'Despite playing hard, the team lost anyway. Every single game.' The short sentence stings.
steps.label: Add the short punch

steps.description: Save the strongest point for the last position, where end-focus gives it the most weight: 'They played hard. They fought in every quarter. They lost anyway.' The final words carry the argument.
steps.label: End with the strongest point

blocks.purpose: Warns about the top errors: fragments that just read as mistakes, run-ons, and parallelism broken mid-list, with non-examples of each.

cautions.detail: A fragment only works as a rhetorical choice when the reader can tell it is deliberate — usually because it is very short, follows a complete sentence, and clearly echoes it. A stray phrase on its own just reads as a typo.
cautions.rightExample: The storm passed by morning. Then silence.
cautions.title: Deliberate vs. accidental fragments
cautions.wrongExample: Walking home because the bus was late.
cautions.exampleNote: The right example is two words the reader instantly understands as deliberate. The wrong one looks like a missing piece.

cautions.detail: A run-on occurs when two or more complete sentences are joined with no punctuation or connector. Blurred structure blurs persuasion: the reader cannot tell which idea to weigh.
cautions.rightExample: The plan was bold. It was also risky.
cautions.title: Run-ons kill impact
cautions.wrongExample: The plan was bold it was also risky.
cautions.exampleNote: The run-on makes both ideas run together; the corrected version gives each its own punch.

cautions.detail: In a list, once you start a pattern (for example, all -ing verbs), every item must keep it. One mismatched item breaks the rhythm and the reader's trust.
cautions.rightExample: We came, we saw, we listened.
cautions.title: Parallelism broken mid-list
cautions.wrongExample: We came, we saw, listening to every word.
cautions.exampleNote: Keep the same form for every item in the series.

cautions.detail: Rhetorical grammar bends conventions on purpose, not by accident. Before you break a rule, make sure you can build the plain, correct sentence first — then decide that the broken version works harder.
cautions.rightExample: Wrinkled. Stained. Perfect anyway. (three fragments with no preceding full sentence)
cautions.title: Don't transfer 'stylistic' to every context
cautions.wrongExample: Using fragments in a lab report conclusion to sound dramatic.
cautions.exampleNote: In formal reporting, complete sentences are the effect you want.

data.flagIntro: Deliberate grammar choices work only when the reader senses they are deliberate. These three errors are the ways 'artistic license' turns into an actual mistake.
data.footerNote: Rule of thumb: a fragment is a choice only if the reader can tell. If a careful reader would call it an error, fix it.

blocks.purpose: Targets the #1 mistake — mistaking any short sentence for an intentional fragment — and reveals why the intuition failed.

choices: It is a deliberate fragment, because it is very short and echoes the complete sentence before it.
It is a deliberate fragment, because all short sentences are stylistic fragments.
It is a run-on, because two ideas appear in the same spot.
It is a complete sentence, because a period was used.
data.commonErrorLabel: Mistaking every short sentence for a deliberate fragment
data.correctReasoning: A deliberate fragment follows a complete sentence and echoes it in a compressed form, so the reader feels the punch instead of noticing a missing piece. 'Then silence.' gives the reader the aftermath in two words — deliberately incomplete, and clearly so.
data.context: A student writes about a storm passing: 'The storm passed by morning. Then silence.'
data.question: Why is the short second sentence 'Then silence.' a deliberate rhetorical fragment rather than an error?
data.recoveryTip: Ask: does the short piece follow a complete sentence and echo it? If yes, it can be a deliberate fragment. If it stands alone or leaves the reader confused, repair it.

trapReasons.1: Short is not the test — many short sentences are complete, and some fragments are accidental errors.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: The intuition fails because it uses the wrong test: length. Shortness is not what makes a fragment deliberate. What matters is that the fragment follows a complete sentence, clearly echoes it, and leaves no confusion about what is missing — the reader instantly supplies the meaning.

statements.feedback: Run-on: two independent clauses jammed together. Split them or add a connector.

statements.context: It follows a complete sentence about the museum visit.
statements.feedback: Deliberate fragment: it echoes the previous sentence and lands like a drumbeat.

statements.context: The list starts with -ing verbs, then breaks the pattern.
statements.feedback: Broken parallelism: keep every item in the same form to build rhythm.
statements.text: We spent the day hiking, swimming, and then the picnic.

statements.context: The main point arrives at the very end.
statements.feedback: Periodic sentence: the build-up creates suspense, and the payoff lands last.
statements.text: If we wait another year to fix the roof, the whole gym closes.

statements.context: A dependent clause standing completely alone.
statements.feedback: Accidental fragment: 'Because...' cannot stand alone, and there is no complete sentence before it to echo.

statements.context: One subject, one verb — it is short, but complete.
statements.feedback: A complete short sentence: subject and verb are both there. Short does not mean broken.

data.summaryBody: A deliberate fragment is short, follows a complete sentence, and clearly echoes it. A run-on jams complete sentences together. Length is never the test — completeness and clarity are.

rows.detail: Choose word order, clause type, and sentence shape on purpose.

rows.detail: Structure blurs, so the persuasion blurs with it.

rows.detail: Same words, different staging, different weight.
rows.value: Periodic builds up to the point at the end; cumulative gives the point first, then adds detail.

checks.prompt: Which statement best defines rhetorical grammar?
checks.answer: Choosing grammatical structures on purpose to create an effect on the reader
checks.rationale: Rhetorical grammar is defined by intent: the writer selects word order, clause type, or sentence shape because of the effect it produces, not by accident or by rigid rule-following.
checks.hint: Think about the word 'rhetorical' — it means aimed at an audience's reaction.
choices: Choosing grammatical structures on purpose to create an effect on the reader
Following every grammar rule exactly as written in all writing
Adding as many clauses as possible to make sentences longer
Avoiding fragments and run-ons no matter what the situation is
checks.focus: Identifying what rhetorical grammar means (choosing structure for effect)

checks.prompt: A writer produces this sentence: 'If we do not protect the forest now, the birds, the streams, and the shade will be gone.' Which technique is this, and why?
checks.answer: Periodic sentence — the main point is saved for the end
checks.rationale: The main point arrives only after the conditional build-up, which is the defining feature of a periodic sentence — the suspense resolves at the end.
checks.hint: Ask: where does the reader finally get the main point?
choices: Parallel structure — all clauses match in form
Fronting — a key phrase is moved to the start
Deliberate fragment — a short punchy incomplete sentence
Periodic sentence — the main point is saved for the end
checks.focus: Matching a sentence's structure to its rhetorical technique

checks.prompt: A student, arguing for a later school start, writes: 'The research is clear. Plain and simple.' The second piece — 'Plain and simple.' — is best described as which of the following?
checks.rationale: A deliberate fragment follows a complete sentence and echoes it in a compressed form, so the reader feels the punch instead of noticing a missing piece. 'Plain and simple.' echoes the idea of clear research in three words — deliberately incomplete, and clearly so.
checks.hint: One test: does it contain two complete sentences jammed together, or is it just short on purpose?
checks.focus: Telling an intentional fragment from a run-on error

checks.prompt: Rewrite this flat sentence so the strongest idea lands at the end, using only the words given and adding at most a comma and a period: 'Silence came after the rage.' Write your reordered sentence.
checks.rationale: End-focus says the reader weighs last words most heavily, so 'rage' must move to the front and 'silence' must be the final word.
checks.hint: Front the loudest idea, and let the quiet word land last.
checks.focus: Producing the persuasive word order for a short sentence
